1	# research-project — running an algorithm against ground truth
2	
3	## 1. The core loop — iterate on the algorithm, and *show* every step
4	
5	For every substantive algorithmic change, in this order:
6	
7	1. **Reproduce & diagnose — visually, first.** Start from the actual inputs.
8	   Render the current behaviour and *look* at it before theorising. If a
9	   decision hinges on a measurable fact (a colour/intensity split, a threshold,
10	   an over-reach, a distribution), write a **throwaway diagnostic and measure
11	   it** — do not guess.
12	2. **Prototype in the scratchpad.** Build the change as a standalone script
13	   first. Do **not** touch tracked code yet.
14	3. **Show a comparison in the chat.** Surface a rendered **[ original | result ]**
15	   side-by-side — and **[ … | ground truth ]** wherever scoring applies —
16	   directly in the conversation (render it inline, don't just link a path). The
17	   **picture leads**; numbers (accuracy metrics, the target quantity) come
18	   *after* it as confirmation, **never instead of it**.
19	4. **Get a read, then commit to the approach.** Only once the visual result is
20	   right do you wire it into the tracked code. If a call is genuinely ambiguous
21	   or is the owner's to make, ask **one** targeted question; otherwise proceed on
22	   a sensible default and state what you chose.
23	5. **Wire it in fully** — see *Definition of done* (§5).
24	6. **Record it** as a numbered iteration note — what was wrong, what changed, the
25	   metric delta, and **what you tried and rejected** (§5).
26	
27	### Show, don't just tell
28	- Every algorithmic change is presented as a rendered comparison against the
29	  original, and against ground truth when scoring is involved. Prefer a clean,
30	  purpose-built **results figure** over a wall of metrics.
31	- The presentation render is usually **not** the debug overlay. Favour a thin,
32	  semi-transparent style that keeps the underlying data readable (thin lines,
33	  mostly-transparent fills), and give a matched object the **same colour in the
34	  result and the ground-truth panels** so over-/under-reach is obvious at a
35	  glance. Tag objects with small ids that key into the metrics table.
36	- **Never draw an annotation in a colour the underlying signal itself carries.**
37	  A mark in the signal's own colour disappears exactly on the objects it exists
38	  to mark, so the figure looks cleanest where the method is least verified. Pick
39	  the overlay palette against the data's own colours (and keep the choice
40	  guarded, if the render is scripted), not by aesthetic preference.
41	- **Show where the method breaks, not only where it works.** The overlay is a QA
42	  tool before it is a result: point at the misses, the fragmentation, the cases
43	  handled badly, and make each claim explicit and checkable ("this outline is
44	  what I'm counting as an object; that one has no outline — it was missed") so
45	  the owner can disagree with a specific claim rather than a general impression.
46	- **Say which of the numbers you just reported are trustworthy, where you report
47	  them.** Every quantity a project reports sits somewhere on a spectrum from
48	  "measured and validated" to "indicative at best" — a quantity derived from a
49	  low-resolution crop, one still inflated by a known failure mode, a split that
50	  rests on a single threshold. State that boundary *inline, beside the number*,
51	  not in a separate caveats section a reader meets after they have already
52	  written the number down. A number quoted without its caveat is read as
53	  trustworthy.
54	- Throwaway renders and diagnostics live in the scratchpad; only the **final
55	  artifact and the code that regenerates it** get committed.
56	
57	### Interaction cadence
58	- **Keep the owner in the loop with pictures**, proactively, and ask a question only when a
59	  decision is genuinely theirs or the request is ambiguous — never to confirm work you can
60	  verify yourself.
61	- **Finishing a unit of work** — leave it committed and pushed, so it can be reviewed or
62	  resumed from a fresh session.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## 2. Ground truth — user-provided, annotated, **never invented**
67	
68	- **The owner's annotations are the ground truth.** Every change is validated by
69	  agreement against them, not against your own expectation of the answer.
70	- **Ground truth is annotated, never fabricated.** Do not invent labels to make a
71	  dataset scorable. If a dataset lacks the annotation a given harness needs, it
72	  does not go into that harness (see §9 on validation tiers).
73	- **Separate source-of-truth from generated artifacts.** The hand-annotation is
74	  the source; the machine-usable ground-truth (registered masks, parsed labels,
75	  normalized tables) is **generated from it and regenerated on demand** — never
76	  hand-edited, because the generator overwrites it. To fix ground truth, **fix
77	  the source annotation (or the extraction code) and regenerate**, then re-score.
78	- **Make extraction deterministic and self-checking.** Same annotation → same
79	  derived ground truth. Pin the things a human counted (number of objects,
80	  number of regions) as assertions/tests so a silent extraction regression fails
81	  loudly.
82	- **Auto-detect annotation conventions from the data**, don't hard-code a
83	  per-input flag. When the owner uses more than one annotation scheme over time,
84	  detect which scheme an input uses from the ink/markup itself. Record the
85	  **conventions** (what each colour / mark / region means) in a durable doc; they
86	  are requirements, not incidental.
87	- **Verify the annotation actually parses before trusting a score.** Inspect two
88	  things: did the markup parse into the labels you expected, and did the derived
89	  ground truth land correctly on the raw input (registration / alignment)? Keep
90	  the review overlays.
91	
92	---
93	
94	## 3. Inputs — a small, similarly-formatted learning set
95	
96	- Projects like this begin with a **small learning set of similarly-formatted
97	  inputs** (same modality, same acquisition regime, same annotation convention).
98	  That is a hazard as well as a feature: it is small enough to overfit (§4).
99	- **State the input format explicitly** (dimensions, modality, contrast
100	  convention, expected content per input) so a mismatched new input is diagnosed
101	  fast. Keep a one-line-per-input table.
102	- **Name the primary target regime and what is out of scope.** A different
103	  regime (inverted contrast, far denser or sparser content, a different scale)
104	  is a *transfer* problem, not the main path — treat it as such until explicitly
105	  in scope.
106	- **Scale-awareness is a first-class concern.** An algorithm tuned for one
107	  input scale (e.g. a zoomed view of a few objects) often fails on another
108	  (a wide field of many). Know which regime you are tuned for, and measure the
109	  gap on the other rather than pretending it's covered.
110	
111	---
112	
113	## 4. Do not overfit the learning set
114	
115	These are **hard constraints** — a change that violates one gets reverted even
116	if it improves a metric.
117	
118	- **No single-input special-casing.** Every rule must generalise across the set.
119	  If a fix only helps one input, say so and either generalise it or drop it.
120	  Never key logic on a specific input's identity/filename.
121	- **Keep decision rules free of the very prior you are trying to measure.** If
122	  the project measures quantity *X*, no rule may bake in an assumed value of *X*
123	  (that turns the measurement into an assumption). Prefer rules expressed in
124	  terms the input **measures for itself** over fixed constants.
125	- **Prefer scale-free rules over pixel/absolute constants.** Where a constant is
126	  unavoidably tied to the current data's scale/resolution, **isolate and label
127	  it** as scale-dependent so it is the first thing revisited on new-scale data.
128	- **Name the hard constraint the task cannot trade away**, and tune to it first —
129	  some projects have a metric whose cost dominates all others; hold it at its
130	  required level before optimising the softer metrics underneath it. Make it
131	  explicit so a later tuning pass doesn't quietly trade it away.
132	- **Keep a registry of domain assumptions, each with a failure mode.** Choices
133	  that encode a prior about the *subject or the instrument* (not pure
134	  processing) are named, located in the code with an inline tag, and given an
135	  explicit "how it fails on mismatched data" note. When a new input looks wrong,
136	  the first diagnostic is *"which assumption did this input break?"*. Flag the
137	  thinly-supported ones (e.g. calibrated on a single example) honestly.
138	- **Guard the wins with regression tests.** An input the owner has blessed as
139	  "very good" must not silently regress when you tune for another. Pin its score.
140	
141	---
142	
143	## 5. Repeatable improvement iterations — the numbered notes, and *definition of done*
144	
145	Each accepted change is recorded as a **numbered iteration note** (pick a short
146	tag and stick to it, e.g. `R1, R2, …`) in a running method-narrative doc, so
147	**the next session does not re-derive what this one already learned.**
148	
149	An iteration note captures:
150	- **What was wrong** (the observed failure, ideally with the diagnostic that
151	  showed it).
152	- **What changed** (the rule/parameter and why, in scale-free terms where
153	  possible).
154	- **The metric delta** — before/after, per input, on the real scoring harness.
155	- **What you tried and rejected, and why** — this is what stops the next session
156	  (or the next model) from walking back into the same dead end.
157	
158	### A metric's definition is part of its identity
159	
160	Write down what each reported metric actually counts, and treat **re-defining
161	one as the owner's call, never a tuning step**. A definition change is uniquely
162	silent: the column keeps its name and its units, so every number ever recorded
163	under it *looks* comparable while the quantity underneath has moved. When a
164	definition does change, the history is **re-measured, never re-labelled** — rerun
165	the old inputs under the new definition, or mark the old numbers as belonging to
166	the old one. Carrying both definitions' numbers in one series under one name is
167	the failure this rule exists to prevent.
168	
169	### A raw measurement is comparable only inside one calibration
170	
171	When each input carries its own scale (a per-image conversion factor, a per-run
172	sampling rate, a per-source unit), a raw absolute quantity means something
173	different in every input. **Aggregate and compare only normalized quantities** —
174	a density, a ratio, a per-unit rate — never the raw number, and never a mean
175	spanning two sources that differ in more than scale (a different instrument,
176	subject or protocol changes *what* is measured, not just how much of it fits in
177	frame). Group the rollup by source and say what the grouping is for.
178	
179	The conversion factor is a **measurement of that input**, not a constant: read it
180	off the input itself, never infer it from a stated setting or borrow it from a
181	neighbour. It lives in exactly one place in the code — a second copy is a second
182	calibration, and whichever copy a given script happens to read wins silently. An
183	input offering nothing to measure the factor from is **not** quietly dropped:
184	mark it uncalibrated *with the reason*, report only its scale-free quantities,
185	and leave it visible as a known gap.
186	
187	### Definition of done for an accepted change
188	- **Source updated — never the generated artifacts.** (Regenerate them.)
189	- **Artifacts regenerated** with the committed generators.
190	- **Tests green**, and the **scoring deltas reported** (per input, per metric).
191	- **Committed with a clear message and pushed**, so the work is reviewable and
192	  resumable from a fresh session / another machine.
193	- **Learnings cached**: the iteration note above, plus a pointer/update in the
194	  session warm-up doc or the relevant reference doc **if the map or procedure
195	  changed**.
196	
197	---
198	
199	## 6. Research phases, and spikes vs the main path
200	
201	- **Separate work into explicit phases**, each with a bounded deliverable, and
202	  say which phase a piece of work belongs to. Defer the hard/advanced piece
203	  explicitly rather than half-building it — e.g. get an intermediate output
204	  trusted before building the final quantity that depends on it.
205	- **Distinguish research spikes from the maintained pipeline.** Exploratory
206	  scripts are worth keeping for reference, but the repo map must make clear what
207	  "the pipeline" actually is versus what was an older spike, so a new session
208	  doesn't mistake a dead branch for the main path.
209	- **Keep a "known open items" / deferred list** so the boundary between "done",
210	  "deferred by choice", and "not yet attempted" is never ambiguous.
211	
212	---
213	
214	## 7. Reading & summarizing source articles
215	
216	When a paper, tool, or reference method matters to the project:
217	
218	- **Write a self-contained notes file so the source never has to be re-read.**
219	  Capture everything algorithmically relevant: the exact method/pipeline and its
220	  parameters, the definitions and formulae, calibration details, and **sanity-check
221	  values** you can validate your own outputs against.
222	- **Capture the method that exists only inside a figure.** Part of a source's
223	  actual procedure is often drawn rather than written — a panel's inset, an
224	  annotated overlay, a legend. Extract and describe it in the notes; a summary
225	  built from the prose alone silently omits it, and the omission is invisible
226	  until someone re-opens the source.
227	- **Write down what the source *fails* to say**, as an explicit gap list — the
228	  parameters, thresholds and units it never states. Recording an absence is what
229	  stops the next reader re-opening the source to hunt for something that was
230	  never in it. The intake is done when the notes make the original redundant, and
231	  a stated gap is part of that.
232	- **Explicitly record where your approach diverges from the reference and why.**
233	- **State what you deliberately omitted** (material not relevant to the
234	  algorithm — e.g. procedural/experimental setup detail, incidental statistics,
235	  acknowledgements) and that you cross-checked against the full text — so a later
236	  reader trusts the summary is complete for its purpose.
237	- Note that upload paths for source PDFs are **session-specific and won't
238	  persist**; the notes file is the durable artifact, not the upload.
239	
240	---
241	
242	## 8. Extracting images — samples vs illustrations
243	
244	- **Samples** are inputs you will run the algorithm on; **illustrations** are
245	  figures that explain a method or a definition. Keep the two roles distinct and
246	  store extracted figures alongside the notes that reference them.
247	- **Render documents with a library, not an assumed system binary.** The
248	  environment often lacks common tools (e.g. a PDF rasterizer such as poppler /
249	  `pdftoppm`); use an in-process library instead. Locate embedded raster images
250	  and render just the region you need, at a zoom high enough to read fine
251	  annotation, with a little padding to catch ink drawn outside the frame.
252	- **Verify identity when an extracted image should match an existing input**
253	  (e.g. an annotated crop over an original) by an exact pixel diff — so you know
254	  an annotation set is a labelling of the *same* data, not a new input.
255	
256	---
257	
258	## 9. Fetching more sample data from the outside
259	
260	- **Grow the corpus from public sources that match the input regime.** Curate and
261	  **rank candidates by fit** = modality match × ground-truth availability × ease
262	  of access, and record licence and provenance for each.
263	- **Make ingestion a committed, repeatable fetch script**, not a manual download,
264	  so anyone can reproduce the corpus.
265	- **Respect the two validation tiers — and don't mix them:**
266	  - **Full ground truth** (per-item annotations) → scores the *algorithm's
267	    detailed output* (overlap / detection) on the real harness.
268	  - **Aggregate label only** (a published summary number, no per-item
269	    annotation) → validates the *summary quantity* the project reports, and
270	    nothing finer.
271	  Wiring an aggregate-only dataset into the detailed-overlap harness would force
272	  you to **fabricate annotations**, which violates §2. Keep a separate,
273	  mask-free validation path for those sets.
274	- **External data is rarely drop-in.** Expect a scale/regime gap (§3) and
275	  *measure* it with the appropriate tier rather than assuming the corpus is
276	  covered.
277	
278	---
279	
280	## 10. Environment limitations — stay lightweight
281	
282	- **A fresh container has nothing installed.** Assume dependencies must be
283	  installed each session, and keep the dependency set **small and lightweight** —
284	  favour a compact set of core libraries over heavy frameworks (e.g. large ML
285	  stacks) that are slow to install and awkward to run anywhere.
286	- **When a heavy or learned approach is genuinely the right tool, treat it as a
287	  gated, isolated route** (documented, opt-in, scoped to the cases that need it)
288	  rather than a new baseline dependency — and prove the lightweight route is
289	  exhausted first.
290	- **Route around missing system binaries with libraries** (see §8). Document the
291	  exact install lines and any "install ad hoc, not in requirements" tools in the
292	  warm-up doc.
293	
294	---
295	
296	## 11. Getting — and evaluating — algorithm ideas from the owner
297	
298	The owner will suggest algorithms and directions to try next. Treat these as
299	first-class experiments:
300	
301	- **Take the suggestion seriously even when the project has declared a direction
302	  "exhausted."** A suggestion may belong to a *different family* than everything
303	  tried so far, which is exactly when it can break a wall the previous family
304	  couldn't.
305	- **Evaluate it the same way as any change**: diagnose the wall it targets, build
306	  the evidence that the wall is real (or isn't), prototype, and show a comparison.
307	- **Beat the naive baseline, or drop it.** A more sophisticated or signal-driven
308	  method is only worth adopting if it *measurably* out-scores the simple/uniform
309	  baseline — sophistication is not accuracy when the guiding signal is noisy or
310	  penetrates the structure unevenly. Keep the roles of a signal distinct, too: a
311	  feature that is excellent for *visualising or validating* a structure can be
312	  wrong for *defining* it — gating the output directly on such a signal can erode
313	  the very structure you are measuring. (1)
314	- **Document the outcome fully**, including the routes that hit a wall and *why*
315	  (name the specific trade-off or signal that defeated them). If the idea needs
316	  capabilities the environment won't allow (§10), record the concrete route to
317	  try when that changes, so the thread is resumable rather than lost.
318	- **Complementary routes are not competitors.** Two methods can attack the same
319	  problem from different angles; keep both documented and say how they relate.
320	
321	---
322	
323	## 12. Record cross-domain applicability **out-of-band**
324	
325	When a sub-step of the algorithm plausibly applies to **another problem** beyond
326	the current task, record it as a **short pointer in a dedicated side document** —
327	a direction worth attention, not a validated claim. **Keep this speculation out
328	of the algorithm itself**: code and inline comments stay strictly about the task
329	at hand and its stated assumptions. Add an entry whenever you build or
330	substantially change a sub-step.
331	
332	---
333	
334	## 13. Continuity across sessions
335	
336	The owner works across many sessions and machines. Every session should end in a
337	**resumable** state.
338	
339	- **Commit and push** finished units of work; leave the project runnable from a
340	  clean checkout.
341	- **Maintain a session warm-up doc** (the "read this first" map): what the project
342	  is, how to run it, where the tuned parameters and the deep rationale live, and
343	  the current numbers. It should let a new session skip re-reading the whole
344	  codebase.
345	- **Maintain a continuation guide**: where things stand, exact run commands, the
346	  tuned parameters and *why they exist*, and the open items. Keep the headline
347	  metrics current in it.
348	- **When the owner asks for a different way to do something, capture the new way
349	  durably — don't just do it this once.** A correction to *how* work is done (how
350	  results are shown, what command to run, a naming/format convention, a step to
351	  always take or skip) is a standing preference, not a one-off. Fold it into the
352	  warm-up doc — or a reference doc linked from it. Prefer editing the doc that
353	  already owns that topic over adding a stray note; if the change contradicts
354	  what's written, replace it and say what changed. The test: *could a fresh
355	  session, with only the warm-up doc, reproduce this new behaviour?* If not, it
356	  isn't captured yet.
357	- Follow the repo's **branch/commit/PR conventions**: develop on the named
358	  branch, commit with clear messages, push; don't open a PR unless asked.
359	
360	---
361	
362	## 14. Reviving a prior session to **enhance this document** (not to continue the research)
363	
364	Some of the owner's process preferences live only in the **dialogue of earlier
365	Claude Code (web) sessions**, not in any committed file. If the owner revives
366	such a session and points it at this playbook, here is the instruction for that
367	revived session:
368	
369	> **Your job in this revived session is to mine our conversation for *process and
370	> working-style preferences*, and fold them into this playbook — NOT to continue
371	> the research task itself.**
372	> Re-read the whole dialogue and extract only the durable, project-agnostic
373	> signal about *how the owner wants research run*: how they want results shown;
374	> what they praised or rejected about the workflow (not just the algorithm);
375	> ground-truth and annotation conventions; anti-overfitting rules they insisted
376	> on; how they want articles summarized, images extracted, and external data
377	> fetched; environment constraints they flagged; and how they hand off algorithm
378	> ideas. For each item, strip out anything specific to this project's subject
379	> matter and generalise it to the class of "run a CV/analysis algorithm over
380	> similarly-formatted inputs, scored against user ground truth, improved in
381	> reviewable iterations." Then propose additions/edits to the relevant numbered
382	> section above (merge, don't duplicate; keep the principle-first phrasing). Show
383	> the owner a diff of what you'd add and confirm the wording before committing.
384	> **Do not run or modify the research pipeline.** If a preference contradicts what
385	> is already written here, surface the conflict for the owner rather than silently
386	> overwriting.
387	
388	To make revival productive, when the owner asks for it they should say **which
389	session(s)** to revive (a link or a description) and, if possible, what topic the
390	process discussion centred on — so the revived session knows where in the
391	transcript to look.

You are auditing Claudinite pack prose in /home/user/Claudinite. Read these files fully: packs/web-scraping/RULES.md, packs/headless-browser/RULES.md, packs/executable-requirements/RULES.md, packs/spec-driven-product/RULES.md, packs/chrome-extension/RULES.md, packs/static-website/RULES.md, packs/web-speech/RULES.md.

Context: every rule in a RULES.md is loaded into every session of every repo declaring the pack, so prose is rationed. A skill (packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md) loads only when its activity is under way, and a skill may now carry a `paths:` frontmatter (glob list) so a PreToolUse guard holds any Edit/Write under those files until the skill is loaded. The question for each rule: should it stay always-on prose, or be extracted into a skill (existing or new), and if so, is that skill path-scoped (name the globs) or activity-scoped (name the trigger)?

Rubric. A rule STAYS as prose when it is working discipline that can apply in any session at any moment, is short, and a session cannot know in advance it will need it. A rule is an EXTRACTION CANDIDATE when (a) it only matters while editing a nameable file class or folder (path-scoped), or (b) it only matters during one nameable activity (release, migration, scraping a new source, wiring a parser), especially if several rules in the file share that activity, or (c) it is long procedural text. Also note rules that describe rather than instruct (how a mechanism works) — those are candidates for deletion to a README, not a skill. For each file also list the existing skills in that pack (ls packs/<pack>/skills) so you can point candidates at an existing skill where one fits.

Output, per pack, a compact table: | Rule (its bold subject, verbatim) | Verdict: stay / extract→<skill name, existing or new> / describe-only | Scope: paths: <globs> or activity: <trigger> | One-line reason |. Then a two-sentence summary per pack: how many rules, how many candidates, and the strongest extraction (which rules, into which skill, with globs). Be precise and terse; do not edit any file.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, size the links (how many PRs, what each one's diff is predicted to touch and the automerge policy that prediction becomes) and write the chain to survive a policy park, a red CI or a PR closed unmerged, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers a dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. 1	# macOS
2	
3	## The app bundle is assembled, not built
4	
5	- **SwiftPM builds a binary; nothing builds you a `.app`.** `swift build -c release` yields an
6	  executable — the bundle (`Contents/MacOS/<exe>`, `Contents/Info.plist`,
7	  `Contents/Resources/`) is assembled by your own script. Keep that script the single place the
8	  bundle's shape is defined, so the local build and CI produce byte-identical layouts.
9	- **Commit one high-resolution icon master and generate the `.icns`** in the build script (`sips`
10	  to each size into an `.iconset`, then `iconutil -c icns`). Both tools ship with macOS, so the
11	  repo carries one PNG instead of ten, and the icon can't half-update.
12	- **A menu-bar-only app is `LSUIElement: true`** in `Info.plist` — that, not code, is what removes
13	  the Dock icon and the main window.
14	- **Pin `LSMinimumSystemVersion` to the same OS version the package's `platforms:` declares.** They
15	  are two independent claims about the same floor, and only one of them is enforced at launch.
16	
17	## TCC and the Hardened Runtime are two different gates — know which applies
18	
19	- **Reaching for a protected resource** — give it its own **usage-description string** in
20	  `Info.plist`, the text the user consents to; without one the app is killed rather than prompted.
21	  Capabilities that feel like one feature take separate keys — an app that listens *and*
22	  transcribes needs `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and `NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription`, or
23	  is killed at whichever it forgot — and only *some* resources also need a codesign entitlement,
24	  and only under the Hardened Runtime.
25	
26	- **Notarization requires the Hardened Runtime** (`codesign --options runtime`), and under it a
27	  resource-access exception must be granted explicitly by entitlement — device capture
28	  (`com.apple.security.device.audio-input`, camera) is the classic one. So **turning on
29	  notarization can silently break a capability an ad-hoc build had**, because the ad-hoc build was
30	  never running under the restriction. Ship the entitlement in the same change as the runtime flag.
31	- **Capabilities gated purely by TCC plus their usage string need no entitlement at all** (speech
32	  recognition is the worked example). Adding one you don't need is noise; omitting one you do need
33	  is a runtime failure no build step catches.
34	- **Do not enable the App Sandbox on the Developer ID track.** The sandbox belongs to the Mac App
35	  Store lane, needs a different (Apple Distribution) certificate, and silently removes
36	  capabilities the direct-download build has — distributed notifications, for one.
37	
38	## Speech recognition leaves the machine unless you say it must not
39	
40	- **`SFSpeechRecognizer` streams audio to Apple's servers by default.** On-device recognition is
41	  opt-in, and the opt-in is a property of the **request**
42	  (`request.requiresOnDeviceRecognition = true`), not of the recognizer — so it has to be set on
43	  every request the app builds, and a new call site added later starts out server-side. Nothing in
44	  the build says which mode ran; the difference is only visible in what left the machine.
45	- **The opt-in is only honourable where the locale's model is installed.** `supportsOnDeviceRecognition`
46	  is per-recognizer and false until then, and requiring on-device recognition where it isn't
47	  supported fails the request rather than quietly falling back — so check it and decide the degrade
48	  deliberately (refuse the feature, or say plainly that this locale would transcribe off-device).
49	- Speech is TCC-gated, so it needs its usage string and **no** entitlement — see the section above.
50	
51	## Keep signing and notarization an optional, secret-gated lane
52	
53	- **The unsigned path must stay a working path.** Gate the Developer ID + notarization steps on the
54	  signing secrets being present, and ship an **ad-hoc-signed** artifact when they aren't. Make
55	  signing a required step and every fork, and every build in a repo whose secrets aren't set, goes
56	  red for a reason unrelated to the change.
57	- **An ad-hoc signature cannot be notarized.** They are separate lanes, not degrees of the same
58	  one: only an identity-signed bundle can be submitted to the notary service. Don't write a
59	  pipeline that "tries" to notarize whatever it just signed.
60	- **Notarize the distributed container, then staple it** (`notarytool submit --wait`, then `stapler
61	  staple` and `stapler validate`). Stapling is what makes the download open offline without a
62	  round-trip to Apple; skipping it works on your machine and fails on a user's.
63	- **In CI, an imported identity must be in the searchable keychain list.** Creating an ephemeral
64	  keychain, importing the `.p12` and setting the key partition list is not enough —
65	  `codesign` searches the *user's keychain list*, so the new keychain has to be added to it or the
66	  identity is simply not found.
67	- **Say out loud, in a build annotation, which lane ran.** "No signing secret — publishing an
68	  ad-hoc build" turns a silently-degraded artifact into a visible one.
69	
70	## Distribution and the Gatekeeper story you owe the user
71	
72	- **A drag-to-install DMG is a staged folder, not Finder scripting.** Stage the `.app` beside a
73	  symlink to `/Applications`, drop the icon in as `.VolumeIcon.icns`, flag the folder as having a
74	  custom icon, and let `hdiutil create` carry it through. Anything that automates Finder to lay out
75	  the window is fragile in CI and unnecessary.
76	- **Write the Gatekeeper bypass for the OS your users are on.** macOS 15 removed the
77	  right-click → *Open* bypass; the current path is System Settings → Privacy & Security →
78	  *Open Anyway*, or `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <app>`. An install doc that still says
79	  right-click → Open reads as broken software.
80	- **A notarized build should need none of that** — if your README's manual-bypass section is the
81	  one users actually follow, the signing lane isn't running.
82	
83	## Assume the user's Mac has no developer toolchain
84	
85	- **Diagnostics belong inside the shipped app**, or in a script using only what ships with macOS.
86	  Anything requiring a compiler on the user's machine is a diagnostic that will never be run.
87	- **`command -v swift` does not test for a Swift toolchain.** `/usr/bin/swift` exists on every Mac
88	  as a stub that pops the *"install the command line developer tools?"* dialog when invoked — so
89	  the probe passes and the script asks the user to install several gigabytes of Xcode. Gate on
90	  `xcode-select -p >/dev/null 2>&1`, which fails quietly when the tools are absent.
91	
92	## Exit paths: `applicationWillTerminate` is not "every exit"
93	
94	- **`NSApplication` installs no signal handlers.** `NSApp.terminate` (menu Quit, ⌘Q, the
95	  logout/shutdown Apple Event) runs `applicationWillTerminate`; a bare `SIGTERM` (Activity
96	  Monitor's Quit, `killall`), `SIGINT` or `SIGHUP` kills the process with **no** teardown. Route
97	  them through a `DispatchSourceSignal` into `NSApp.terminate` — and set `signal(sig, SIG_IGN)`
98	  **before** `resume()`, or a signal arriving in the gap still takes the fatal default.
99	  `SIGKILL`, Force Quit and a crash stay uncoverable; name that as residual risk rather than
100	  claiming coverage.
101	- **An uncaught Objective-C exception is an exit path too.** It aborts the process, so no teardown
102	  runs; a framework call that *raises* (rather than throws) is therefore a resource-release bug as
103	  well as a crash. Swift cannot catch `NSException` — a tiny Objective-C target of your own is the
104	  only trap, and it is only safe around calls that validate before mutating.
105	
106	## Sleep, wake, and deferred work
107	
108	- **There is no "the machine is back" notification.** `NSWorkspace.didWakeNotification` also fires
109	  for a dark/Power-Nap wake with nobody there. Fan in the several signals that a real return emits
110	  (wake, screens wake, session became active, the screen-unlocked distributed notification) and
111	  **coalesce them** — a genuine return fires a burst, and each must not schedule its own work.
112	- **Coalesce with an id, not a boolean.** A single `pending` flag deadlocks: something invalidates
113	  the timer, the timer clears the flag, and whichever ordering loses leaves the next wake either
114	  unable to schedule or double-scheduling. Hold the in-flight work's id; a stale timer compares its
115	  captured id and returns.
116	- **`asyncAfter` work scheduled before sleep fires immediately on wake.** Give every intentional
117	  stop a generation counter, capture the generation when scheduling, and abort in the closure if it
118	  moved — otherwise deferred work reacquires resources on the way *into* sleep or before the
119	  machine has settled. When cancelling in-flight work, reset the latches beside it too, or they
120	  stay stuck and block everything after.
121	- **Measure a span that includes a sleep with `Date()`, not `ProcessInfo.systemUptime`.** The
122	  monotonic clock does not advance while the machine sleeps — which is exactly the span you are
123	  trying to measure. Use `systemUptime` for the opposite question ("how long, while we were
124	  awake").
125	
126	## Holding a device the user can unplug
127	
128	- **Release the device on every path where capture ends.** A process that dies with its IO proc
129	  still registered can leave some USB devices wedged until physically re-plugged. This is necessary
130	  and *not sufficient* — a device can also wedge below the user-space audio daemon, where no
131	  teardown of yours helps.
132	- **Never construct a capture engine to ask whether a device exists.** Materializing an input node
133	  opens the default device and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device; a retry ladder built on
134	  that is not a cheap probe but an open/close plus an aggregate create-and-destroy, repeated for as
135	  long as the hardware is missing. Query the HAL's device properties instead — a property read
136	  opens nothing and can be sampled forever for free. The churn is observable rather than
137	  theoretical: each hidden aggregate appears in the HAL as `CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`, so
138	  what a retry ladder is really doing can be counted instead of argued about.
139	- **Presence is not usability, at either layer.** Mid-teardown a device enumerates as alive with an
140	  unreadable name and a **zero** sample rate. Require a nonzero rate and a sane channel count, and
141	  judge the *system default* input — a healthy device behind a broken default is not one you can
142	  capture from. One layer up, the engine lies in the opposite direction: with the input torn down,
143	  the input node's `outputFormat(forBus: 0)` still reports a plausible 48 kHz while its
144	  `inputFormat` reports 0, so a guard written against the wrong one waves through starts that
145	  cannot succeed — read both and require them to agree. Whatever a new probe reads, ask what that
146	  field says while the device is absent.
147	- **A duration is a claim about a span you observed.** "It has been present for N seconds" is only
148	  as good as the observation behind it: a state maintained by a timer must be **seeded at start**
149	  (a repeating timer does not fire immediately) and **invalidated across any gap** — a sleep is a
150	  gap, and carrying a settle clock straight through one makes the gate inert on exactly the
151	  transition it was built for. Model "not observed" as its own state, distinct from "absent", and
152	  key the span on the device's **UID** — an unplug-and-replug, or a swap for a different mic, is a
153	  new arrival that starts its own clock rather than inheriting the departed device's.
154	- **"Started" is not "working".** A running engine delivering buffers of pure silence looks
155	  identical to a healthy one from the inside. Measure what actually arrives, publish a health state
156	  the UI renders, and when a failure mode has exactly one remedy, name **that** remedy rather than
157	  the generic one.
158	- **Compile-green is not a gate for device code.** `swift build` cannot see a raise-vs-throw bug or
159	  a lifecycle race, and both are reachable in the first second of a run. A change here is not
160	  verified until the app has actually launched on a Mac. Reaching the interesting case needs no
161	  hardware theatre: let the display sleep and `coreaudiod` tears its device contexts down seconds
162	  later, which is the same transition as an unplug from the app's point of view.
163

1	# core — working with Claudinite itself
2	
3	- **Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite** — it is vendored, under
4	  `.claudinite/shared/`, and the update flows replace that whole tree. Never edit anything there:
5	  change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.
6	
7	- **Finding a mounted skill, or following a link from inside one you already loaded** — a canon
8	  skill lives at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; there is no flat
9	  `.claudinite/shared/skills/`. When the `Skill` tool announces a per-session flat "base directory"
10	  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
11	  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
12	  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.
13	
14	- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-settings.json`. Nothing
15	  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
16	  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.
17	
18	- **Adding a pack** — run the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions,
19	  re-vendors and scaffolds. Never hand-copy a pack's content into the repo.
20	
21	- **Setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time** — the `adopt-claudinite` skill.
22	
23	- **Deciding which pack owns a lesson** — read `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of
24	  *every* canon pack, never the mounted subset: the mount holds only what this repo declares, so the
25	  pack that owns the territory may be absent and invisible. When the owning pack is merely too
26	  narrow, widen its `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` rather than opening a local pack beside it.
27	
28	- **Judging whether Claudinite is current here** — read the stamp's `engineVersion` and
29	  `packVersions`, never `claudinite.updated` or `ref`: the versioned flows stamp versions and
30	  nothing else, so those two hold the provenance of the last full re-vendor rather than of this
31	  mount, and a member converging nightly reads as weeks stale.
32	
33	- **Answering "why did the mount not update"** — read the member's own artifacts (its declaration,
34	  its stamp, the head sha's runs) before theorizing about a platform setting; propose a settings
35	  change as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.
